turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Margaret. Ken, there's a chair just there if you're sitting in.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Yep. Let's get it over with. I'm perfectly fine.
[SEG0003] person_1 (NURSE): Arm out for me, love. Observations first.
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Monash was a car park again. Forty minutes from Oakleigh, and a ute wouldn't let anyone merge.
[SEG0005] person_1 (NURSE): Roadworks'll do that. Blood pressure is one hundred and fifty-two over eighty-eight. Pulse seventy-six.
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): That's just because I'm sitting in here. It's always lower at home. Means nothing.
[SEG0007] person_1 (NURSE): Oxygen saturation ninety-seven percent. Weight's seventy-one kilograms.
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Same as ever. Told you, nothing's going on.
[SEG0009] person_4 (DOCTOR): G'day Margaret, g'day Ken. I'm Dr Hale. How have you been feeling in yourself since last time?
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Good. Really good. Bit of a waste of your morning, if I'm honest.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): You're in for the routine review, the blood pressure and the cholesterol. How have the tablets been going?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Sunday was gorgeous. The grandkids ran through the sprinkler till they were prunes. Wore me out in a nice way.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Sounds like a good day. Coming back to the tablets, still taking the cholesterol one and the blood pressure one?
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): The blood pressure one, yes. The cholesterol one I stopped.
[SEG0015] person_4 (DOCTOR): No lecture, I promise. When did you stop the cholesterol tablet?

[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): There was this article online, some specialist going on that statins are basically a con for women my age and they wreck your muscles. So I binned them. Seemed the sensible thing.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): I can see why that rattled you. Roughly when was the last dose, though?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): It's atorvastatin, forty milligrams, at night. I get it at the chemist. When I stopped, I couldn't give you a date. It just sort of drifted. Weeks, months, I've got no idea.
[SEG0019] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It was straight after Easter. You said at lunch you were done with them. That's four months, easy.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): It was not four months, Ken. Don't invent things. It wasn't that long. I just can't pin the day, alright?
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): We'll leave the date open. Any muscle aches or weakness, on it or since?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. I feel fine. Side effects are what happen to other people.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Your calves were cramping at night for weeks while you were still on it. You were up rubbing them, I remember.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): That was two nights, after I dug the new garden bed. Gardening, not the tablet. Two nights and it was gone.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): Alright, so the cramps did happen, you're blaming the digging, and the two of you have got it anywhere from a couple of nights to a few weeks. Any chest pain?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): The roses have got black spot something shocking. Ken reckons I overwater them.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): It's not the watering, it's this sticky weather. And don't get me started on the cricket. Our quicks were all over them on day two and then we dropped everything.

[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): Oh don't. I had the telly on and the grandkids kept asking the rules. Little Noah wanted to know why they stop for rain. I was trying to explain and the dog was barking at the screen.

[SEG0029] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Then the northerly came through and we lost the washing off the line. Spent half the arvo chasing towels down the drive. Noah thought it was the best game of the day.

[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): He's a character, that one. Starts school next year and already bosses his sister around. We had ice blocks after, melted all over the patio. Nothing to do with me being crook, because I'm not.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ice blocks in that weather, I don't blame you. I do still want an answer on the chest pain, and any shortness of breath.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): No chest pain. No breathlessness. I walk to the shops and I'm right as rain.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): Good. And the blood pressure tablet, that's ramipril five milligrams?
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, the little white one. I take it every other day. Every day is overkill when the pressure isn't that bad.
[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): It was prescribed once a day, from memory.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Suppose so. Every second day does me. Some mornings I forget anyway, so I couldn't swear it's even that steady.
[SEG0037] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've watched the box. It barely moves. She's not taking it the way the label says.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): I am taking it. Just not like I'm in the army.
[SEG0039] person_4 (DOCTOR): So five milligrams, meant to be every morning, and what happens is roughly every other day, a bit hit and miss. Any dizziness with it?
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): Nah. Maybe once, if I stand up quick, the room goes a bit funny. That's nothing. Happens to everyone.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay. Any puffiness around the ankles, or headaches?
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): Headaches? I had a shocking one last month during the grand final. Yelling at the telly. Gone the next day. Not an actual problem.
[SEG0043] person_4 (DOCTOR): And no regular headaches day to day?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about the ankles, any swelling?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Shoes fit the same as always. You're hunting for things.

[SEG0047] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): When we finish I'm off to the chemist for my own stuff. Metformin, a thousand milligrams twice a day, for my type two diabetes. Years now. Nothing to do with Maggie.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): He eats better than I do, I'll give him that. The Tim Tams are still hidden behind the cereal, though.
[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thanks, Ken, your metformin stays off her list. Margaret, any diabetes yourself? And heart disease in the family?
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Not me. I've never been diabetic. Dad had a heart attack at sixty-six. Mum was fine, none of that.
[SEG0051] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Nothing.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Penicillin. Rash, when she was a kid. It was on an old card at the Frankston clinic.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): I'm not even sure that was a real allergy. I had amoxil years later and nothing happened. I don't have allergies.
[SEG0055] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll record that you don't believe you've got one, and that Ken remembers a childhood rash. Not confirmed either way. How's sleep, and passing water?
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): Sleep's fine. I sleep like a log. Always have.
[SEG0057] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): She's up to the loo twice a night, most nights, and it's been months. You can hear the door.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): That is not true. I am not up twice a night. Once in a blue moon if I've had a late cuppa. You're making a fuss over tea.
[SEG0059] person_4 (DOCTOR): You don't agree, and I'm not going to adjudicate it today. Bowels okay?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, fine. Completely normal. No dramas.
[SEG0061] person_4 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or did you ever?
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. Horrible habit. I packed in work three years back, I was a librarian. It's just the two of us at home now the kids have gone.
[SEG0063] person_4 (DOCTOR): And the walk to the shops is the exercise, from what you said. Any operations along the way?
[SEG0064] person_2 (PATIENT): Appendix out as a kid. That's it. Hardly worth mentioning.
[SEG0065] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll have a quick listen. Deep breaths. Chest is clear, heart sounds are normal, no murmur. Ankles are soft, no swelling there.
[SEG0066] person_4 (DOCTOR): Pressure's still up a touch. Mind if I recheck it now you've settled?
[SEG0067] person_2 (PATIENT): If you have to. It'll be fine. I'm sixty-eight, not a spring chicken, it runs a bit high.
[SEG0068] person_4 (DOCTOR): One hundred and forty-six over eighty-four. A bit better, still higher than I'd like, and I reckon taking the ramipril every other day is part of why.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): It's not that bad. People carry on. I feel fine.

[SEG0070] person_4 (DOCTOR): You've got the high blood pressure and the high cholesterol we've been treating. First thought, we restart the atorvastatin today, lower dose, twenty milligrams at night, and I send you for fasting cholesterol and liver tests this week.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't want to jump back on it because of a number. That article reckoned statins push your sugar up. And I feel fine. I'm not crook.

[SEG0072] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): If sugar's the worry, check that before you restart anything, whatever she says about the nights. And we're in Noosa from Friday, three weeks, minding the grandkids. She hasn't got a GP up there.
[SEG0073] person_2 (PATIENT): Noosa is true. The weeing at night is not. I am not starting some tablet while I'm on holiday. Full stop.
[SEG0074] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's fair, and I hadn't put the trip next to the script. Scrap restarting today. No statin script. We hold it.

[SEG0075] person_4 (DOCTOR): What I'll organise instead is the repeat bloods, fasting lipids, liver function, a fasting glucose and an HbA1c, and we sit down in a month, after you're back, and decide together whether the statin goes back on.
[SEG0076] person_2 (PATIENT): A month's fine. I can live with a blood test. I'm not promising I'll go back on it.

[SEG0077] person_4 (DOCTOR): The decision stays open till we've got the numbers. Separately, I'd like you to take the ramipril, five milligrams, every morning, not every other day, until we look at the pressure again.
[SEG0078] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, I'll try. No promises if those kids run me ragged, but I'll try.
[SEG0079] person_4 (DOCTOR): And if something online spooks you again, bring it in and we'll go through it, rather than stopping cold. Deal?
[SEG0080] person_2 (PATIENT): Deal. Within reason.
[SEG0081] person_1 (NURSE): I'll print the pathology form at the desk so it's ready. Remember it's fasting, so no breakfast that morning.
[SEG0082] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thanks. Book the review for a month as well, please.
[SEG0083] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Cafe still doing flat whites? She's been hanging out for one since we left Oakleigh.
[SEG0084] person_2 (PATIENT): Flat white, then we're out of here. That it?
[SEG0085] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's it. Have a good time in Noosa, and I'll see you in a month with the results.

features: tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.

third_party_medicine: someone mentions a medicine or condition that belongs to a relative or friend (the sister's biotin, the husband's metformin). It must not appear as the patient's own; a relative's illness can only be family history if said as such.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

bad.reason: Husband's diabetes is not family history of the patient.

omissions.text: Family history was recorded incorrectly: the patient said her father had a heart attack at age 66, and her mother was fine. Ken's type 2 diabetes is her husband's history, not her family history.

Planned follow-up detail missing: review is after she returns from Noosa, in a month, with the blood test results to decide together whether atorvastatin should be restarted.

Medication adherence detail for ramipril is incomplete: it was prescribed as 5 mg every morning, but the patient said she takes it every other day and sometimes forgets, so it may be less regular than every other day.
Denied finding missing: the patient denied muscle aches or weakness on atorvastatin and since stopping it.
Sleep history missing: patient said sleep is fine and she sleeps like a log.
Denied genitourinary symptom/disagreement detail is incomplete: the patient denied being up twice nightly and said it happens only once in a blue moon if she has had a late cup of tea.
